newsitem.title: USA: Discounters making inroads in U.S. book market.
newsitem.headline: Discounters making inroads in U.S. book market.

text.p: Americans bought more books in 1996, but the gains went largely to discount stores, not bookstores, according to a study presented Sunday by the American Booksellers Association.

Americans purchased 1.06 billion books for adults last year, three percent more than in 1995, according to monthly surveys of 16,000 U.S. households conducted by a market research firm for the association's Book Industry Study Group.

Of all book purchases made last year, discount stores such as Wal-Mart Stores Inc, Kmart Corp and Dayton Hudson Corp's Target accounted for nine percent, up from seven percent in 1995, the survey reported.

By contrast, the percentage of purchases consumers said they made at independent and small chain bookstores fell to a new low of 18 from 20 percent, while the share of large chain bookstores slipped to 25 from 26 percent.
Market share held steady for all other outlets, including 18 percent for book clubs, the survey showed.
"The pattern is that independent and small chain bookstores continued to lose market share," said Barrie Rappaport, who managed the survey for the study group.

As recently as 1991, independent and small chain bookstores accounted for nearly a third of U.S. book purchases, but they have lost market share rapidly in the face of aggressive expansion by huge chains, such as Borders Group Inc, Barnes & Noble Inc, Crown Books Corp and others.
As usual, about 51 percent of all books bought last year were popular fiction.
Cooking and craft books accounted for the second largest share of purchases at 10 percent, followed by general non-fiction at nine percent and religion at seven percent.

Psychology/recovery titles made up six percent, as did technical/science/educational books. The remaining 11 percent was divided among art/literature/poetry, travel/regional interest, reference and all other categories, the survey said.
Perhaps reinforcing the trend toward discount store buying, the survey said that price became a more important factor last year in consumers' book purchasing decisions.

The key decision factors remained the book's topic, its author and a recommendation from a friend, but five percent of consumers last year said price entered into their decision, as well, up from just two percent in 1995, the study said.

By age category, Americans aged 55 and up accounted for 32 percent of book purchases, the largest portion. Those aged 45 to 54 accounted for 23 percent; aged 35 to 44 for 25 percent; aged 25 to 34 for 16 percent; and under 25 for four percent.
Consumer purchases of childrens' books also jumped by five percent to 535 million copies in 1996. Half of that was fiction books and a quarter coloring books.
